titleStmt.title: One-level and Two-level Scheduling for Real-time Systems

analytic.title: One-level and Two-level Scheduling for Real-time Systems

application.desc: GROBID - A machine learning software for extracting information from scholarly documents

div.p: This paper proposes and analyzes the one-level and the two-level scheduling approach. The one-level scheduling uses one scheduling policy for scheduling all tasks, whereas the twolevel scheduling uses one scheduling policy for the scheduling of high priority tasks and other for the scheduling of low priority tasks. Both scheduling approaches use Earliest Deadline First and Rate Monotonic scheduling algorithms, the two-level scheduling only for scheduling of higher priority tasks. The focus of both approaches is the scheduling of the Imprecise Computation Model tasks. The Imprecise Computation Model trades off the quality of computations with the timeliness. It decomposes each task into a mandatory part and an optional part. Only the mandatory part is required to complete by task's deadline. The scheduling of Imprecise Computation Model tasks that minimizes the total-weighted error is considered. The onelevel scheduling is based on an extension of mandatory parts that minimizes the total-weighted error. In order to minimize the total-weighted error the two-level scheduling uses modified Algorithm WNTU by the low level scheduler. The analysis of both approaches is provided including complexity, response time analysis and simulations. Based on the theoretical foundations and the results of simulations the use of one-level and two-level scheduling is recommended under certain assumptions. Single preemptive model is assumed.

div.head: I. INTRODUCTION
div.p: The correctness of a real-time system depends as much on the tasks completing by their deadline as on the logical correctness of their results. In a real-time system, every task must produce a result within specified time interval. In the traditional model (precise) every task must meet its deadline (if a task misses the deadline a timing fault is said to have occurred) and in a valid precise schedule, every task is precisely scheduled. In a dynamic situation (transient overload, etc.) where the available time and resources are not enough for the computation to complete within the deadlines, there may be still enough resources to produce approximate results within the specified time intervals. For many applications, approximate results are acceptable, but some penalties may apply. The Imprecise Computation Model (ICM) ( [1], [2]) is motivated by this idea, which gives flexibility to trade off precision for timeliness. During dynamic situations, the ICM helps prevent missed deadlines and provides graceful degradation by ensuring that an approximate result of acceptable quality is available whenever the exact result cannot be obtained in time.
The precise task system used in this paper consists of a set of n independent, preemptable tasks, TS = {T 1 , T 2 ,…, T n }.

Each task T i is characterized by the quadruple T i = (r i , d i , e i , p i ) where r i , d i , e i , and p i denote the task's ready time, relative deadline, execution time and the task's period, respectively. The ICM task system used in this paper consists of a set of n independent, preemptable tasks, ITS = {τ 1 , τ 2 ,…, τ n }. Each task τ i is characterized by the quintuple τ i = (r i , d i , m i , o i , p i ),

where m i and o i denote mandatory and optional execution times, respectively. In the ICM model, the task τ i is partitioned into a mandatory part M i and an optional part O i (the j th job of the task τ i is partitioned into a mandatory part M ij (M ij = M i , ∀j) and an optional part

Further, we focus only to the tasks without loss of generality. The optional part O i is dependent on the mandatory part M i , the mandatory part M i always executes before the optional part O i . The ready time and deadline of these parts are the same as those of the task τ i . Only the mandatory part is required to complete by the task's deadline. The optional part does not have to be complete (if there is no available processor's time) or even does not have to be started. The task systems TS and ITS are assumed to be synchronous. A task system is said to be synchronous if all ready times are zeros, otherwise a task system is asynchronous. This implies that all ready times of our task systems are assumed to be equal to zero, r i = 0. The tasks' deadlines are assumed to be equal to tasks' periods d i = p i . Without loss of generality, integer values for all tasks' parameters are assumed as provided in [3]. The synchronism of task system and integer parameters facilitate the analysis which, in this case, can be performed on the limited time period equal to hyperperiod H, the least common multiplier of all periods in TS or ITS, H = lcm (p 1 ,..., p n ). div.head: II. ONE-LEVEL SCHEDULING
div.p: Define scheduling where a scheduler applies the same scheduling policy for all tasks in task system, as one-level scheduling. This scheduling approach is a logical consequence of scheduling precise task system TS. All classical, wellknown, scheduling results [5] can be applied for the one-level scheduling of precise task system TS.

The one-level scheduling is not able to distinguish mandatory from optional subtasks and built-in precedence relation. In one-level scheduling approach all tasks, mandatory or optional, are scheduled in one level by one scheduler, SC. This implies that the ICM model needs to be adapted for the one-level scheduling. There are many ways how the ICM model can be modified for the one-level scheduling, e.g. all optional subtasks can be mapped to a new task, to all optional subtasks can be assigned priorities that are lower than the lowest priority among the mandatory subtasks. We propose a method that extends the mandatory execution times. It is based on the creation of new, single task system that comprises, in a way, mandatory as well as optional subtask system. After the creation, the single task system is scheduled by SC. We denote that single task system as M' and call it new mandatory subtask system. It represents the extension of mandatory subtask system M, the execution times of M' are extended in comparison to the execution times of M. The optional subtask system, O, is not directly scheduled. It is included in the schedule of new mandatory subtask system, M'. The creation of M' and its relation with one-level scheduler SC is depicted in Fig. 1. Basically, the one-level scheduling of ICM can be divided in two parts: extension of mandatory subtask system and scheduling of extended mandatory subtask system using one of scheduling algorithms. We assume the use of EDF and RM scheduling algorithms. There are different metrics that can be used in the extension of mandatory subtask system and we use the minimization of total-weighted error, provided in [6].
The one-level scheduling for ICM may be divided in the following steps:

• generation of a new task system, M', for a given ICM task system and scheduling algorithm (EDF or RM): o determination of the maximum extension, ext MAX , of mandatory execution times; o determination of the extension for each mandatory subtask M i , ext i , in a way that the total-weighted error is minimized; • precise scheduling of new task system M' by EDF or RM.

div.head: III. TWO-LEVEL SCHEDULING
div.p: Define scheduling where a scheduler schedules tasks on two different levels, possibly by different scheduling policies, as two-level scheduling. Here two-level scheduler ISC, a hierarchy of two prioritized schedulers, SC 1 and SC 2 , is considered. This two level scheduling is a natural scheduling approach for scheduling of ICM task system ITS.

Scheduler ISC is able to distinguish mandatory and optional subtask system, i.e. it applies separate, possibly different, scheduling policies for mandatory and optional subtask system. High level scheduler SC 1 is responsible of the scheduling of mandatory subtask system, whereas low level scheduler SC 2 is responsible of the scheduling of optional subtask system. Two-level scheduling produces schedules on two levels. On the high level mandatory subtask system is scheduled, while on the low level optional subtask system is scheduled. The high level has to ensure processor time and its assignment to the low level. Scheduler ISC, its hierarchy and scheduling of ICM task system ITS is depicted in Fig. 2. In this paper we assume the use of EDF and RM by SC 1 in scheduling of mandatory subtask systems. As already mentioned, different scheduling policies optimizing different metrics may be used by SC 2 in scheduling of optional subtask systems. The same as for the one-level scheduling the imperative is the minimization of total-weighted error. This implies the scheduling policy used by SC 2 has to ensure the execution of optional subtask system in a way that the totalweighted error of ITS is minimized. On the high level mandatory subsystem M is scheduled and processor time for optional subtask system O has to be ensured. This is done by adding a new mandatory subtask M n+1 to M and as the result a new mandatory subtask system M' is created. M' must not harm the schedulability of M and the execution time of M n+1 is assigned to optional subtask system O. The maximum possible execution time for M n+1 should be determined; the time intervals assigned to M n+1 should be determined and optional subtask system O should be scheduled over found time intervals in a way that the totalweighted error is minimized. This should be done for the use of EDF and RM by SC 1 . SC makes use of Theorem 2 from [6] which says that feasible schedules generated by EDF and RM have the same busy periods, i.e. idle periods. This implies if mandatory subtask system M is schedulable by EDF and RM, optional subtask system O is scheduled in the same way at the low level regardless of the scheduling algorithms used by the high level. For the optimal scheduling of optional subtask systems modified Algorithm NTU and Algorithm WNTU provided in [6] are used. Algorithm NTU and Algorithm WNTU are presented in more details in [11].
The two-level scheduling for ICM may be split in the following steps:
• schedulability of M by EDF and RM;

• calculation of idle intervals based on the processor availability and the workload of M (Algorithm 2, [6]); • calculation of optimum schedule of optional subtask system (modified WNTU and NTU, [6]). Note that the optimal schedule of optional subtask system must be generated offline. The mandatory subtask system M is scheduled online by SC 1 . In the case of idle period the control is switched to SC 2 where the optional subtask system is scheduled according to the predefined schedule. The flexibility of the ICM model has been lost in the two-level scheduling.

There are different ways of scheduling of precise task system TS by the two-level scheduling. All precise tasks can be scheduled by high level scheduler SC 1 , precise tasks can be divided in two groups, etc. In the paper the case in which each precise task of precise task system TS is decomposed in two parts, two atomic subtasks T i = {T i1 , T i2 }, i=1,…,n, is considered. We have precise task system TS decomposed in two subtask systems, TS = TS 1 U TS 2 , where TS 1 = {T 11 ,T 21 ,…, T n1 } and TS 2 = {T 12 ,T 22 ,…, T n2 }. It is assumed that subtask system TS 1 is scheduled by SC 1 and subtask system TS 2 scheduled by SC 2 , i.e. that all subtasks from TS 1 have higher priorities than tasks from TS 2 . EDF and RM are assumed for SC 1 and SC 2 schedulers.

div.head: IV. COMPLEXITY AND RESPONSE TIME ANALYSIS
A. Complexity
div.p: As already mentioned one-level scheduling comprises generation of the new task system and its precise scheduling using EDF or RM by SC. Accordingly, the complexity of onelevel scheduling can be divided in two parts: the complexity of generation of the new task system and the complexity of scheduler SC, i.e. the scheduling algorithm used. The generation of the new task system is reduced to BKP which is, in our case, solved using a branch and bound algorithm, Algorithm 5.1. The precise scheduling is done by EDF or RM. In the worst case, a branch and bound search algorithm must explore every node in a state space. Thus, the worst case complexity of branch and bound is the size of a state space. In our case the size of the state space is equal to (o 1 +1)*...*(o n +1) minus a number of combination where subject to part of equation ( 2) is not true (
div.formula: ¦ = ≤ n i MAX i i ext o n 1
div.p: ). The generation of the new task system is done once, offline, before the scheduling takes place for both scheduling algorithms. Because of it, the complexity of extension process should not be critical. The complexity of EDF and RM depends on their implementations. The implementations can be generic or on top of a kernel of operating system as discussed in [12]. The implementations can depend on a number of priorities supported and data structures available. EDF is a dynamic, while RM is a static scheduling algorithm which implies that priorities for RM are calculated just once, whereas for EDF they need to be re-calculated. According to RM, tasks are assigned fixed priorities in inverse proportion to their periods, shorter period higher priority. Determination of the priorities of task system with n tasks for RM can be reduced to ordering the task system according to their periods. This implies that the complexity of the RM priority assignment corresponds to the complexity of a sorting algorithm as provided in [13], i.e. O(nlog(n)). According to EDF, tasks are assigned dynamic priorities in inverse proportion to their absolute deadlines, shorter absolute deadline higher priority. Calculation of the absolute deadlines and determination of the priorities of task system with n tasks for EDF can be done in the same way as for RM, i.e. O(nlog(n)). In [14] an EDF implementation with sorted lists used for the queue with the complexity O(n 2 ) has been proposed and an efficient implementation of EDF has been provided in [15]. A lot of different implementations of RM exist and it has been included in many high technology projects including Global Positioning Satellite and International Space Station as stated in [5].

Scheduler ISC comprises two schedulers: high level scheduler SC 1 and low level scheduler SC 2 . The complexity of ICS depends on the complexity of these schedulers. SC 1 is based on EDF or RM scheduling algorithms and its complexity is the same as the complexity of SC (one-level scheduling). The complexity of SC 2 is based on the complexity of algorithms applied on the low level, i.e. modified Algorithm NTU and Algorithm WNTU. Modified Algorithm NTU proposed in [6] has the same complexity as Algorithm NTU provided in [11] O(n 2 ): sorting the tasks in descending order, O(nlog(n)); the first step takes linear time, O(n); and calculations take O(n 2 ). It is possible to improve Algorithm NTU and decrease its complexity. According to [11] the complexity is O(nlog(n)) if sorting is included or O(n) if no sorting is needed. The complexity of modified Algorithm WNTU is O(nlog(n) + kn) taking into account that NTU does not require tasks sorting [11].

div.head: B. Response time analysis
div.p: The response time analysis of one-level scheduling is based on response time analysis of scheduling algorithms used, i.e. EDF and RM. The response time analysis of RM is the basis for exact schedulability tests for RM and it is provided in [16]. Since the schedulability of EDF is not directly related to its response time analysis no special attention has been given to it. The analysis of EDF response times can be easily done based on the results provided in [16].

In general, two-level scheduling is not concerned with response times. It is more interested in optimization of a certain scheduling objective. Scheduler ISC is waiting for tasks' deadlines to finish their execution. A successful end of an optional subtask execution in SC 2 or a task's deadline represents the task's response time for the two-level scheduling.

div.head: V. SIMULATION AND ANALYSIS
div.p: In order to simulate schedulers, tasks and their execution a simulation framework has been developed and implemented in MATLAB. MATLAB® is a MathWorks high-level language and interactive environment for numerical computation, visualization, and programming. A set of synchronous periodic task systems, Set(Ĳ), is used in the simulation. Each task system of Set(Ĳ), Ĳ, comprises nine tasks, i.e. Ĳ = {T 1 , …, T 9 }, T i = (r i , d i , e i , p i ), 1i9, where r i ,=0, d i = p i , e i ‫א‬ [0, p i ], p i =i+1. This implies that each task T i can be characterized by the pair T i = (e i , p i ). As additional parameters, each task system has its own ID and weight. The IDs are assigned to tasks as follows: for T i , ID i = i, 1i9. The weights are in inverse proportion to tasks IDs, i.e. for task T i , w i = 10 -i, 1i9. A total number of combinations for

Moreover, empty subset is included too, a subset where e i =0 for any i. Set of periodic task systems Set(Ĳ) is used for the generation of all mandatory and optional subtask systems in simulations. Note that some task systems of Set(Ĳ) are not schedulable at all, they have processor utilization greater than 1 and they are not well suited for simulations. For the purpose of simulations all algorithms mentioned in this paper have been implemented: BPK solving algorithm (Algorithm 5.1), idle intervals finding algorithm (Algorithm 5.2), modified NTU and WNTU. In addition, RM and EDF basic schedulablity tests have been implemented as well as calculation of total-weighted and total error.

M and O subtask systems used in simulations have been created from Set(Ĳ) based on processor utilization. E.g., M(0.1U0.2) and O(0.2U0.4) means that all task systems of Set(Ĳ) with processor utilization between 0.1 and 0.2 represents the set of mandatory subtask systems, Set(M), and all task systems of Set(Ĳ) with processor utilization between 0.2 and 0.4 the set of optional subtask systems, Set(Ĳ). Finally, each task system of Set(M) is combined with all task systems of Set(O) which gives the set of ICM task systems, Set(ICM), used in the simulations.

We divide the workload of M and O subtask systems in three parts: light workload (0 < U 0.2), medium workload (0.2 < U 0.4) and heavy workload (0.4 < U 1). All combinations for M and O subtask systems have been simulated and analyzed. The most important results are presented in the paper.

div.head: A. One-level Scheduling
div.p: The objective of one-level scheduling analysis is to analyze schedulability, processor utilization of ICM task systems, optimizations of weighted tasks systems and total-weighted error for both scheduling algorithms, EDF and RM, with respect to different workloads of M and O subtask systems.

For task systems with small processor utilizations i.e. where processor utilizations are less than the least upper bound to processor utilization does not matter which scheduling algorithm is used, EDF or RM. If processor utilizations of task systems are close to the least upper bound to processor utilization the use of EDF provides better results than RM. EDF achieves better schedulability, higher processor utilization and total-weighted errors. The main reason is the least upper bound to processor utilization of EDF which is greater than the least upper bound to processor utilization of RM. A typical behavior of processor utilization of one-level scheduling is depicted in Fig. 3 where M+O task system represents a task system obtained by merging appropriate M and O subtasks in a single task. EXT_EDF and EXT_RM represent newly task systems generated with respect to EDF and RM and the minimization of total-weighted error, respectively. The number of task systems used in this simulation is 135500. The utilization of EXT_RM follows the utilization of M+O approximately up to the 1000 th task system and then oscillates between 0.6 and 0.75 (with overshoots and undershoots). On the other side, the utilization of EXT_EDF follows the utilization of M+O approximately up to the 1.92x10 4 th task system and further it oscillates between 0.83 and 1. This is clear demonstration that EDF shows better behavior. Since all M subtask systems are schedulable it implies that all newly generated task systems with respect to both, EDF and RM are schedulable too. The oscillations and their sizes are caused by the fact that the one-level scheduling tries to extend all instances of a mandatory subtask as much as possible and if it is not possible for all instances it does not extend the mandatory subtask (even if there is available time for extension for some of the instances).

Errors start earlier for EXT_RM task systems and they have greater values in comparison to EXT_EDF. For the EXT_RM task systems errors start around the 1000 th task system, whereas for EXT_EDF task systems around the 1.92x10 4 th task system. The total-weighted error for EXT_EDF is mostly below 500 weighted time units with rare overshoots to 1000-2000 weighted time units, and for EXT_RM it is mostly below 1500 with frequent overshoots to 4000-5000 and rare overshoots to 14000 weighted time units. Fig. 4 depicts totalweighted error (TWE) for the EXT_EDF and EXT_RM task systems. The results of simulations segmented per mandatory and optional subtask systems' workloads are provided in Table I. The decision which scheduling algorithm provides better results, EDF or RM, is based on the schedulability, the utilization and the total-weighted error.

div.head: B. Two-level Scheduling
div.p: According to Theorem 5.2 provided in [6] if a M task system is schedulable by SC 1 regardless of scheduling algorithm used, resulting high-level schedules, S EDF and S RM , have the same idle intervals. This implies that SC 2 in both cases has the same processor availability and the same O task system to be scheduled by Algorithm WNTU. Finally, it implies the same behavior for both scheduling algorithms used by SC 1 if a M task system is schedulable by both EDF and RM at SC 1 . The same behavior is granted until the utilization of M task systems reaches the least upper bound to processor utilization for RM. Between this value of utilization and the least upper bound to processor utilization for EDF, M task systems and therefore ICM task systems are schedulable only by EDF at SC 1 . If the utilization of M task systems exceeds the least upper bound to processor utilization for EDF, M task systems aren't schedulable by EDF neither by RM. The better results produced by EDF in comparison to RM are present just for heavy workload of M task systems. Table II shows the comparison of EDF and RM for the two-level scheduling. As for the one-level scheduling, the algorithm showing better behavior is written in the table.

div.head: C. Comparison of One-level and Two-level Scheduling
div.p: The objective of comparison is the identification of strengths and weaknesses of both scheduling approaches and the recommendation of their applications. This is done by different simulations. In the analysis schedulability, processor utilization and total-weighted error are included. For the twolevel scheduling the utilization cannot be defined as for the periodic task systems. For the ICM task systems we define the processor utilization as σ where a i is the amount of assigned time to the task system. The behaviors of one-level and two-level scheduling for the same workload of mandatory and optional subtask systems are depicted in Fig. 5 and Fig. 6, respectively. The workload of this simulation for mandatory subtask systems is M(0.2U0. 4) and O(0.7U0.72) for optional subtask systems. Since the utilization of M task systems is greater that the least upper bound to processor utilization for EDF and RM for all tasks participated in the simulation all task systems are schedulable by SC and ISC using both EDF and RM. The utilization of EXT_RM task systems in one-level scheduling cannot follow the utilization of M+O task systems and it oscillates around 0.7 (Fig. 5). The utilization of EXT_EDF follows ideally the utilization of M+O task systems, then on reaching the least upper bound (1) it is immediately decreased and finally increases with oscillations (Fig. 5). The oscillations and their size, as mentioned above, depend on mandatory and optional subtask systems characteristics as well as on the extension process.

The utilization of High-EDF (EDF used by SC 1 ) and High-RM (RM used by SC 1 ) in two-level scheduling have completely the same behavior and they follow the utilization of M+O task systems until it reaches 1 with oscillations during the complete set of task systems (Fig. 6). The oscillations are smaller than the one-level EXT_EDF oscillations (especially than EXT_RM oscillations) and no immediate undershoot which is caused by the tasks' granularity and inability to extend the M task systems (all instances of a task need to be extended). In two levelscheduling just certain (any ready) O task instances may be executed. The continuous oscillations of utilization of High- EDF and High-RM are caused by the two-level scheduling phenomenon.

As expected, the one-level scheduling, SC, based on RM has the largest total-weighted error and it is not considered further. The total-weighted error in the case of EDF and SC oscillates immediately between 0 and 1000 with some overshoots above 1000 (Fig. 7), whereas in the case of twolevel scheduling, ISC, the total-weighted error linearly increases with oscillations to 500 (Fig. 8). The situation is slightly better than for the EDF and SC which is surprising since the utilization is in the favor of two-level scheduling. This is caused by the fact that the one-level scheduling extends all instances of tasks in decreasing order of their weights, whereas the two-level scheduling optimizes the execution of optional tasks in predefined idle intervals. The two-level scheduling suffers from the two-level phenomenon that is described later in the paper. The simulation results are presented in two tables. In the first table, Table III, the results of both, one-level and twolevel scheduling for RM are presented. For RM, the two-level scheduling shows better results. Still, there are some workloads (light) where both scheduling approaches can be useful. Scheduling approaches that provide better results are marked in the tables. The second table, Table IV, shows the results for EDF. For the light and the medium workloads of mandatory subtask systems both approaches show almost the same behavior. Because of the two-level scheduling phenomenon, the onelevel scheduling achieves slightly better performance. For the heavy workload of mandatory subtask systems the two-level scheduling shows much better behavior.

div.head: D. Two-level scheduling phenomenon
div.p: In general, the two-level scheduling phenomenon says that high-level scheduler by executing a high level task may sometimes prevent low-level scheduler of execution of a low level task even if there is enough available processor time to execute both of them. This is caused by priority approach. In our case the phenomenon is manifested as inability of scheduling ICM task systems sometimes without errors even if there is enough available processor time for their scheduling without errors. It happens when a start of a M task prevents an O task to be executed even if there is enough available processor time.

A task system is most sensitive to this phenomenon at its critical zone. The critical zone of a task system is defined as a time interval from the simultaneous start of all tasks to the end of execution of the lowest priority task. Since we deal with synchronous periodic task systems the worst case is present in the two-level scheduling of all task systems.

Consider an ICM task system, M = { T 9 = (2, 10)} and O = { T 1 = (1, 2), T 8 = (1, 9), T 9 = (1, 10)} with the hyperperiod H = 90. We have U(M) = 0.2 what implies the schedulability of the one-level and two level scheduling and U(M+O) = 0.911 what implies no error for the one-level scheduling using EDF.

In the two-level scheduling, regardless of scheduling algorithms used, each execution of M 1 (T 9 ) task prevents the execution of O 1 (T 1 ). This introduces an error which can be easily calculated. Finally, for the two-level scheduling we have the total error of 9 time units. The part of execution of ICM by ICS using EDF or RM by SC 1 and RM by SC 2 is depicted in Fig. 9 where missed instances of O 1 task are marked. The high level scheduler is based on the use of EDF and RM scheduling algorithms. The complexity, response time analysis, results of simulations and their analysis for both approaches are provided. The focus is put on the ICM tasks and both approaches tend to minimize the total-weighted error.

Because of the minimization the flexibility of ICM is lost in both approaches. For the one-level scheduling the extension needs to be done once before the scheduling, but the scheduling can be done online. The two-level scheduling must be done offline.
The use of a branch and bound algorithm to solve the BKP extension problem makes the one-level scheduling more complex.

Response time analysis of the one-level scheduling for RM is based on classical scheduling results, while for EDF it is missing. The two-level scheduling is focused on the optimization, not on the response times and the tasks' deadlines are considered as their response times.

The simulations of one-level scheduling show better performance of EDF in respect to RM. RM can be successfully used just for light workloads of mandatory and optional subtask systems. The analysis of two-level scheduling provides almost the same results for both EDF and RM scheduling algorithms. EDF provides better results just in the case of heavy workload of mandatory subtask systems. The comparison of one-level with two-level scheduling provides the worst results for the one-level scheduling using RM. The use of EDF by both approaches and the use of RM by the two-level scheduling show the similar behavior. In some cases the one-level provides better results because of the two-level scheduling phenomenon. In the case of heavy workload of mandatory subtask systems the two-level provides better results.
